summary: Builds precise, correctly-applied inheritance vocabulary for 8–10 year-olds: inherited characteristic, acquired characteristic, variation, offspring, trait/characteristic, species, breed, environment (and 'genetic' used only informally, no DNA/gene mechanism at this stage). The load-bearing distinction is inherited (passed from parent to offspring; often visible at birth, but some inherited features, such as a Dalmatian's spots, a baby's final eye colour or a plant's petal colour, appear only as the young grow) versus acquired (gained during life through experience or surroundings, not passed on). It is taught by contrast with sortable plant AND animal examples and justified with the test 'Did it come from the parents, or did it happen to this individual during its life?' ('Would the baby be born with it?' is a useful first check for injuries and learned skills, but it is not proof.)
misconceptions: Believing acquired characteristics are inherited — e.g. a parent's scar, muscles, tan, or trained skill will show up in the offspring (the Lamarckian seed error).
Using 'variation' to mean differences BETWEEN species rather than WITHIN a species.
Treating 'trait/characteristic', 'gene' and 'DNA' as interchangeable, or expecting a genetic MECHANISM at this age.
Confusing 'species' and 'breed' — thinking different dog breeds are different species.
Thinking offspring are identical copies of a parent, missing the 'vary and are not identical' idea.
Assuming any feature an animal HAS is inherited, without checking whether it was gained during life.

activities.title: Family album: tap a feature, name it, test whether it's passed on
steps: Look at a scene of families: a dog with a litter of puppies, a plant with its seedlings, and a human family, each showing visible features.

Point to or tap a puppy's coat colour and say the term and definition: 'inherited characteristic — passed from parent to offspring' (optionally the matching colour on the parent lights up to make the link visible).
Point to or tap the parent dog's torn ear or a person's scar and apply the test: 'Would the baby be born with this? No — it was gained during life, so it is acquired and is not passed on.'
Compare several puppies across the litter and use 'variation — differences within the same species; they are not identical'.

Pin each remaining term to a picture you can see: offspring (the young, one or many), species (same kind that can breed together), breed (a variety within a species), environment (surroundings that can also shape a feature).
Answer a lift-the-flap check such as 'Is a learned trick inherited?' → 'No — acquired.'
activities.insight: Each vocabulary word attaches to a concrete example, and the invisible line between 'came from the parents' (inherited) and 'happened during this individual's life' (acquired) becomes visible and testable. Only inherited features are passed from parent to offspring, though the young can gain their own acquired features later.

activities.title: Sort the feature cards and justify each placement
steps: Take feature cards — eye colour, scar, petal colour, pierced ear, seed shape, natural fur type, a learned skill/trained trick — and place each into an INHERITED bin or an ACQUIRED bin.
Say aloud or write the reason for each placement, e.g. 'A scar is acquired because you got it during your life, so puppies won't be born with it.'
For any card you get wrong, ask 'Did it come from the parents, or did it happen during this individual's life?' and move it.
In a second round, sort examples of within-species VARIATION (e.g. different sizes and markings among the same litter or among seedlings of one plant).
activities.insight: Learners deploy the vocabulary to justify a decision, proving they own the inherited↔acquired boundary rather than just recognising definitions.

activities.title: Describe a dog and its puppies using the words
steps: Tell or write about a dog and its puppies using inherited, acquired, variation, and offspring as you go.
Describe one thing the puppies were born with and one thing an individual picked up during its life, using the right word for each.

Answer follow-up prompts: 'Could the environment change the coat colour at all — and what would you call that?'; 'One puppy learned to sit on command — inherited or acquired, and why?'; 'Use variation in a sentence about just the puppies, not comparing them to another animal'; 'What's the difference between the same breed and the same species?'
activities.insight: Correct use in a live, self-generated description — not a recited definition — shows genuine command, especially sorting traits that came from the parents (inherited) from those gained during life (acquired), and saying clearly whether 'variation' compares individuals of one species or different species.

checkQuestion: Tell me about a dog and its puppies, using these words as you go: inherited, acquired, variation, offspring. Describe something the puppies were born with, and something one of them picked up during its life — and use the right word for each.
checkAnswer: The child uses each term correctly in a meaningful sentence: the puppies are the dog's offspring; they inherited traits such as coat colour (inherited characteristic); a scar or a learned trick is acquired (acquired characteristic); the puppies differ from one another in size and markings (variation).
